item.title: Beginning Strength and Conditioning: Bridging Science and Practice (EMI & Bilingual)
item.description:
As an Adjunct Lecturer (兼任講師) at National Taiwan Normal University (NTNU / 臺師大), I focus on transforming a passion for fitness into a scientifically grounded practice. My teaching methodology bridges the gap between exercise science and real-world application in the Beginning Strength and Conditioning (初階肌力與體能訓練) course.

To cultivate a diverse and international learning environment, this course is offered in two dedicated sessions:

  • 🕒 Friday 13:20 ~ 15:20 (EMI): English as a Medium of Instruction
  • 🕒 Friday 15:30 ~ 17:30 (Mandarin): Chinese Instruction

Foundational Science, Applied Technique, Program Design!

Course Teaching Methodology

Bridging the Gap Between Science and Application

In my course, Beginning Strength and Conditioning, I guide students through the “Gold Standard” of the industry—the NSCA’s Essentials of Strength Training and Conditioning. My approach ensures that students don’t just memorize terms but truly understand the “why” behind the “how” of lifting and athletic performance.

This instructional video provides an overview of how the course is structured to prepare students with foundational knowledge in anatomical adaptations, biomechanics, and proper lifting mechanics.

Watch Course Description on YouTube

Core Pillars of My Instruction

Based on my teaching demonstration, the curriculum is built around three critical domains, delivered effectively in both English and Chinese:

  1. Foundational Science: We explore anatomy, bioenergetics, and biomechanics. It’s not just about naming muscles; it’s about understanding how the human body generates power and adapts to physical stress.
  2. Applied Technique: From core stability exercises to foundational barbell lifts (squat, hinge, push, pull) and cardiovascular protocols, students practice techniques outlined in our resources to refine their lifting and coaching skills.
  3. Program Design: This is where science becomes art. Students learn to design safe, effective programs for diverse goals—from hypertrophy to strength and aerobic endurance.

Inside the Classroom: Practical Teaching Demonstrations

Translating Movement Science to Lifting Success

A proficient practitioner must be able to analyze posture and movement efficiency instantly. In this segment, I explain how to utilize the three planes of motion (sagittal, frontal, and transverse) and varying lever systems in practical scenarios. By deeply understanding concentric, eccentric, and isometric contractions, students can provide precise verbal cues and drastically reduce the risk of injury.

(Note: In the EMI session, these cues are taught using international standard terminology to prepare students for global contexts.)

Watch on YouTube

Mastering the Initial Framework of Strength Training

Success in strength and conditioning relies on proper assessment and systematic progression. This video captures how I teach students to establish the foundational framework for both their aerobic and resistance training routines.

Watch on YouTube

Long-Term Programming Strategy: The GAS Model

To prevent plateaus and overtraining, one must master the art of periodization. Here, I introduce the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) to illustrate how the human body responds to physiological stress. Students learn to strategically manipulate FITT-VP variables to create sustainable, long-term adaptations.

Watch on YouTube

The Golden Rules of Physiological Adaptation

Generic workouts fail to produce specific results. In this lecture highlight, I break down the three non-negotiable rules of training: Specificity, Overload, and Progression. I place a strong emphasis on the Principle of Specificity, teaching students how to select exercises and energy systems that directly align with unique health or performance goals.

Watch on YouTube

Professional Excellence & Global Readiness

The ultimate goal of this methodology is to ensure students are equipped with world-class strength and conditioning knowledge, ready to apply these principles safely and effectively.

  • Bilingual Advantage: Teaching through both EMI and Mandarin equips NTNU students with local adaptability and international competitiveness.
  • Instructional Focus: Meticulously aligned with NSCA evidence-based guidelines.
  • Industry Expertise: Grounded in my experience as a PhD candidate and holder of NSCA-CSCS*D and ACSM-CEP certifications.

item.title: World Literature English Reading Clubs with Alex Socop
item.description:
Ying-Chu Chen recently participated in an English Reading Club session with Alex Socop that pivoted from technical systems to the biting, ironical landscapes of World Literature. The group gathered to dissect the work of Augusto Monterroso, a master of Latin American flash fiction, focusing specifically on his quintessential fable, “The Monkey Who Wanted to Be a Satirist.”

The discussion focused on Monterroso’s subversive use of the fable tradition to explore the ethical quagmire of the artist. Participants, including Ying-Chu, traced the Monkey’s journey from an eager observer of “human nature” to a silent mystic, paralyzed by the realization that true satire is incompatible with social popularity. The group analyzed the Monkey’s dilemma: his deep understanding of his peers’ flaws—the thievery of the Magpie, the flattery of the Serpent, and the promiscuity of the Hens—rendered him unable to write without wounding the very friends who “feted” him.

The dialogue delved into several sophisticated literary themes:

  • The Moral Paralysis of the Observer: The group questioned whether the Monkey’s eventual silence was an act of empathy or social cowardice, highlighting how intelligence can become a “prison” when one is too aware of the social cost of honesty.
  • The “Mirror” Effect of Satire: Attendees discussed the hypocrisy of an audience that celebrates “truth-telling” in the abstract but recoils the moment a literary mirror reflects their own vanities.
  • The Irony of the “Good Friend”: A central point of debate was the trade-off between social belonging and artistic integrity. By choosing to be a “wonderful person,” the Monkey ultimately became a “failed artist,” eventually drifting into “Mysticism and Love” only to be branded as mad by the society he sought to spare.

By synthesizing Monterroso’s brevity with the complex intellectual and political landscape of the Latin American “Boom” generation, the session successfully challenged participants to consider the role of the intellectual today. It was a high-level discourse that explored how the fear of being “unkind” can lead to a sterilized culture, reminding everyone that the most potent critiques are often those we find hardest to write—and hardest to read.

item.title: Cybernetics English Reading Clubs with Robert McLawhorn
item.description:
Ying-Chu Chen recently participated in an English Reading Club session with Robert McLawhorn that embarked on an intellectual exploration of cybernetics, a profoundly influential, if often misunderstood, interdisciplinary field. The group began by defining the discipline as coined by Norbert Wiener: the study of regulatory mechanisms, communication, and control within complex systems, whether living organisms, machines, or social structures.

The reading group’s discussion transcended the pop-culture caricature of cyborgs. Instead, participants, including Ying-Chu, engaged with the foundational principles that govern how systems self-regulate, adapt, and pursue goals. Their textual analysis centered on the ubiquitous concept of the feedback loop, the mechanism by which a system’s output is “fed back” as input. They dissected seminal works to distinguish between deviation-correcting (negative) feedback, which ensures stability (homeostasis), and deviation-amplifying (positive) feedback, which drives exponential change.

Furthermore, the attendees grappled with the field’s sophisticated evolution, contrasting “first-order” cybernetics (the objective observation of external systems) with “second-order” cybernetics, which compellingly implicates the observer within the system being studied. The group acknowledged that this framework is no mere historical artifact but rather the conceptual progenitor of modern artificial intelligence, systems biology, computational neuroscience, and management theory.

The discussions challenged the participants to synthesize these abstract models and apply them rigorously, collectively exploring how these concepts illuminate cognitive processes, ecological resilience, or the emergent behavior of algorithms. It was a high-level discourse that successfully dissected the complex architecture of control underpinning the modern world.

item.title: Shaping the Future of Bilingual Collaboration: EMI Course Demonstration by Steve Ying-Chu Chen
Career Path English Reading Clubs with Yolanda
item.description:
Steve Ying-Chu Chen recently participated in an English Reading Club session hosted by Yolanda, which embarked on a rigorous intellectual exploration of the modern career trajectory—a domain often reduced to platitudes yet profoundly significant in its complexity. The group began by redefining the concept of a “career” not as a linear ladder, but as a dynamic ecosystem of professional identity, adaptability, and value exchange within an increasingly volatile marketplace.

Under Yolanda’s astute moderation, the discussion transcended the pedestrian clichés of resume polishing or networking tactics. Instead, participants, including Steve, engaged with the foundational principles that govern professional self-regulation and goal attainment. Their analysis centered on the pivotal concept of “strategic agility,” dissecting the mechanisms by which individuals must process market feedback to iterate on their skill sets. They examined the dichotomy between “maintenance learning,” which ensures stability in a current role, and “shock learning,” which is required to navigate the exponential changes driven by technological disruption.

Furthermore, the attendees grappled with the sophisticated evolution of vocational psychology, contrasting the antiquated “organizational” career model (where the institution dictates the path) with the “protean” career model. This latter framework compellingly implicates the individual as the sole architect of their journey, driven by psychological success rather than external metrics. The group acknowledged that this paradigm shift is the conceptual progenitor of the gig economy, the portfolio career, and the rise of personal branding.

The discussions challenged the participants to synthesize these abstract models and apply them rigorously to their own lives, collectively exploring how these concepts illuminate the challenges of AI displacement, the necessity of lifelong upskilling, and the pursuit of purpose. It was a high-level discourse that successfully dissected the complex architecture of professional navigation underpinning the modern world.

item.title: Explorations in Poetic Transcendence with Ruben
item.description:
Steve Ying-Chu Chen recently participated in an English Reading Club session hosted by Ruben, which embarked on a rigorous intellectual exploration of poetic form and its capacity to encapsulate the human condition—a domain often dismissed as mere abstraction, yet profoundly significant in its linguistic and cognitive complexity. The group began by redefining “poetry” not as a static arrangement of verse, but as a dynamic interplay of phonology, semantics, and emotional resonance.

Under Ruben’s astute moderation, the discussion transcended the pedestrian clichés of rhyming schemes or basic imagery. Instead, participants, including Steve, engaged with the foundational principles that govern “poetic economy”—the mechanism by which maximum affect is achieved through minimal, yet precise, linguistic input. Their analysis centered on the concept of “metaphorical salience,” dissecting how poets utilize cross-domain mapping to bridge the gap between tangible experience and metaphysical inquiry. They examined the dichotomy between “formalist precision,” which demands structural rigor, and “negative capability,” the capacity to remain in uncertainties and mysteries without an irritable reaching after fact and reason.

Furthermore, the attendees grappled with the sophisticated evolution of contemporary poetics, contrasting the traditional “mimetic” model (where poetry reflects external reality) with the “expressive” and “objective” models. This latter framework compellingly positions the poem as an autonomous object of inquiry, where the individual’s perception is both the architect and the subject of the literary experience. The group acknowledged that this paradigm shift is the conceptual progenitor of modern experimental verse and the reclamation of oral traditions in the digital age.

The discussions challenged the participants to synthesize these abstract models and apply them rigorously to their own cognitive frameworks, collectively exploring how poetry illuminates the nuances of human empathy, the limitations of literal language, and the enduring pursuit of aesthetic truth. It was a high-level discourse that successfully dissected the complex architecture of verbal art underpinning our shared cultural consciousness.

item.title: Translating Filial Piety: International Sinology English Reading Clubs
item.description:
With funding from the National Taiwan Normal University Library, a recent English Reading Club session led by Ying-Chu Chen embarked on a rigorous intellectual exploration of cross-cultural translation and international sinology. The reading group focused deeply on the book The Westward Journey of Filial Piety (《孝道西遊》), authored by Professor Pan Feng-Chuan, who notably served as his advisor during his studies at the Graduate Institute of International Sinology.

Under Ying-Chu’s moderation, the discussion transcended basic textual analysis to engage with the complex history of how Chinese classics were interpreted by the West. Participants examined the book’s core case study: the translation of the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiaojing) by Western missionaries and sinologists during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. They dissected how translation is never a neutral act, but rather a dynamic process where translators—from François Noël to James Legge—adapted the concept of “filial piety” to fit distinct European contexts, including the Chinese Rites Controversy, imperial literature, and the rise of comparative religion.

Furthermore, the attendees grappled with the sophisticated evolution of international sinology. They analyzed Professor Pan’s proposition that these various translations functioned as a “double-sided mirror.” This framework compellingly illustrates how translated texts reveal shifts in European academic paradigms over time, while simultaneously highlighting diverse interpretations of Chinese culture. The group acknowledged that these historical translations are not mere antiquarian artifacts; they are the conceptual progenitors of modern international sinology.

The discussions challenged the participants to synthesize these historical models and apply them rigorously to the study of cross-cultural exchange. By exploring deep methodological reflections on missionary sinology, the group collectively dissected the complex architecture of how Eastern ethical frameworks were systematically reconstructed in the Western intellectual world.

item.title: Health and Wellness English Reading Clubs with Josh Gracio
item.description:
Starting September 30, 2023, Ying-Chu Chen participated in a comprehensive English Reading Club focused on the multidisciplinary aspects of human health and wellness. Led by Josh Gracio, the group embarked on a three-week intellectual exploration of lifestyle factors, nutrition, and physical activity, grounding their discussions in scientific literature and data.

During the first week, the group examined “A Comprehensive Guide to Health and Wellness for International Students.” Rather than simply reviewing general advice, participants analyzed data and expert insights to understand the unique physiological and psychological stressors faced by students in new environments. This session established a strong foundation for understanding evidence-based wellness strategies.

The textual analysis in the second week centered on “Unlocking the Secrets of Nutrition.” The reading group dissected the significance of balanced diets, moving beyond basic macronutrients to deeply discuss the behavioral mechanisms of portion control and mindful eating. Participants explored how self-regulation and intentionality apply to dietary habits to maintain homeostasis and overall well-being.

In the final week, the discussion transitioned to “The World of Exercise and Physical Activity: A Journey to Motivation, Well-being, and Health Statistics.” The attendees grappled with the psychological and physiological mechanisms that drive exercise adherence. By reviewing current health statistics, the group synthesized how both acute and chronic physical activity positively impact physical health and cognitive function.

These weekly discussions provided a rigorous platform to dissect the complex architecture of human wellness, challenging participants to integrate these scientific frameworks into both everyday life and academic research contexts.
